conditions.name: Alzheimer's disease

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Book an appointment in the next few days

conditions.summary: Progressive loss of recent memory first, with older memories preserved until late. Onset is so gradual that families date it to an event rather than a time, and insight is often lost early.
workup: Cognitive testing with a validated tool
Bloods to exclude reversible causes: TFTs, B12, folate, calcium, glucose
CT or MRI brain
Memory clinic referral
Always ask an informant, not only the patient

exam.step: Watch the patient walk and turn
exam.positive: Reduced arm swing, shuffling, and turning in several steps

exam.step: Test for bradykinesia with finger tapping
exam.positive: Amplitude decrements as the movement repeats

exam.step: Test tone at the wrist with the other arm moving
exam.positive: Cogwheel rigidity, worse on one side

exam.step: Ask to see recent handwriting
exam.positive: Micrographia is often present before the tremor is noticed

labs.test: Review every drug for dopamine blockers first
labs.confirms: Drug-induced parkinsonism is reversible and looks identical

labs.test: Clinical diagnosis: bradykinesia plus tremor or rigidity
TFTs, B12 and copper studies in younger patients

labs.confirms: Response to levodopa is part of the diagnosis

conditions.name: Parkinson's disease

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Book an appointment in the next few days

conditions.summary: Slowness of movement with a resting tremor and stiffness, coming on gradually and worse on one side than the other. Small handwriting and a shuffling turn often appear before the tremor is noticed.
workup: Clinical diagnosis on bradykinesia plus tremor or rigidity
Review every drug for dopamine blockers before diagnosing
Neurology referral before starting treatment
DaTscan only where the picture is genuinely unclear

exam.step: Establish the trajectory with an informant
exam.positive: Stepwise decline rather than a smooth slide

exam.step: Full neurological examination
exam.positive: Focal signs and brisk reflexes are common

exam.step: Blood pressure, pulse and carotid auscultation
exam.positive: The vascular substrate

exam.step: Watch the gait
exam.positive: Often affected early, unlike Alzheimer's

labs.confirms: Both diagnostic support and what you treat

conditions.name: Vascular dementia

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Book an appointment in the next few days

conditions.summary: Cognitive decline from cumulative vascular damage. It classically drops in steps rather than sliding smoothly, and the vascular history and focal signs are what separate it from Alzheimer's.
workup: Cognitive testing
Vascular risk assessment: blood pressure, lipids, HbA1c, ECG
CT or MRI showing small-vessel disease or old infarcts
Aggressive secondary prevention, which slows the trajectory

exam.step: Time a ten-metre walk and count the steps to turn
exam.positive: Gives an objective baseline to compare after tapping

exam.step: Ask about bladder control directly
exam.positive: It is rarely volunteered and completes the triad

exam.step: Brief cognitive test
exam.positive: Slowed thinking rather than the amnesia of Alzheimer's

labs.test: Document the triad and the order it appeared in
labs.confirms: Gait first is what distinguishes it
Ventricles enlarged out of proportion to any atrophy

labs.test: Large-volume lumbar puncture with gait timed before and after

conditions.name: Normal pressure hydrocephalus

triage.label: See a doctor soon
triage.action: Book an appointment in the next few days

conditions.summary: Fluid accumulating in the brain's ventricles at normal pressure, producing a magnetic shuffling gait, incontinence and cognitive slowing. Worth finding because shunting can reverse it, and it is regularly written off as ageing.
workup: Look for the triad: gait first, then bladder, then cognition
CT or MRI for ventricular enlargement out of proportion to atrophy
Large-volume lumbar puncture with gait timed before and after
Neurosurgical referral if gait improves

exam.step: Cough stress test
exam.positive: Leakage on coughing suggests a stress component

exam.step: Abdominal and pelvic examination
exam.positive: Assess for pelvic organ prolapse, palpable bladder (retention with overflow)

exam.step: Screen for red flags
exam.positive: Back pain, saddle numbness or leg weakness raise concern for cauda equina syndrome -- a neurological emergency, not routine incontinence

labs.confirms: Excludes urinary tract infection as a contributing/reversible cause
Overflow incontinence from incomplete bladder emptying
Clarifies the type of incontinence when the diagnosis is unclear or before surgery

conditions.name: Urinary incontinence

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Involuntary leakage of urine -- stress incontinence (leakage with coughing, sneezing or exertion, common after childbirth) or urge incontinence (a sudden strong urge with leakage before reaching the toilet, often with frequency). Frequently under-reported and simply endured, especially by older and postpartum women, due to embarrassment.
workup: Bladder diary
Urinalysis to exclude infection
Post-void residual measurement
Pelvic floor physiotherapy first-line for stress incontinence
Bladder training and antimuscarinics/beta-3 agonists for urge incontinence
Urodynamics if diagnosis unclear or surgery being considered

exam.step: Confirm this is a child in the developmentally appropriate age range, with no memory loss, gait disturbance, falls or confusion
exam.positive: The genuine hallmark distinguishing this benign childhood pattern from an adult neurological cause of incontinence

exam.step: Ask whether this is primary (never dry) or secondary (previously dry) enuresis
exam.positive: Secondary enuresis more often warrants a look for an underlying trigger (stress, urinary infection, constipation, diabetes)

exam.step: Screen for daytime urinary symptoms and constipation
exam.positive: Their presence changes the assessment and management approach

labs.confirms: Screens for infection or glucosuria, particularly for secondary enuresis or if daytime symptoms are present

labs.test: Clinical history and a bladder diary
labs.confirms: Usually sufficient for diagnosis and to guide initial management

conditions.name: Nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting)

triage.label: Routine
triage.action: Discuss with your doctor at a routine appointment

conditions.summary: Involuntary passage of urine during sleep in a child old enough to reasonably be expected to be dry (usually assessed from age 5), genuinely very common and, in the great majority of cases, a benign developmental pattern rather than a sign of neurological disease. Distinct from the dementia/neurodegenerative conditions sharing this bundle (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, Vascular Dementia, Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus): this is a childhood condition with none of the memory loss, gait disturbance, falls or cognitive decline seen in those adult conditions.
workup: Ask about the pattern: primary (never achieved dryness) vs secondary (was dry, now wetting again -- secondary enuresis more often has an identifiable trigger or underlying cause)
Screen for daytime symptoms, constipation, and psychosocial stressors, all of which can contribute
Reassurance and simple behavioural measures (bedtime fluid restriction, scheduled voiding, reward charts) as first-line for younger children
Enuresis alarm therapy or, for older children/short-term needs, desmopressin, guided by current paediatric guidance

redFlags.label: Possible sepsis
redFlags.message: A fever together with confusion, very fast breathing, mottled skin or a collapsing blood pressure can mean infection is affecting the whole body.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Do not wait to see whether it settles.

redFlags.label: Rash that does not fade under pressure
redFlags.message: Spots that stay visible when a glass is pressed on them, alongside feeling unwell, can be a sign of bacteria in the bloodstream.

redFlags.label: Possible severe allergic reaction
redFlags.message: Swelling of the throat or tongue with difficulty breathing after a food, sting, or medicine can close the airway within minutes.
redFlags.action: Use an adrenaline auto-injector if you have one, then call emergency services.

redFlags.label: Reduced consciousness
redFlags.message: Being difficult to rouse, or drifting in and out of awareness, always needs immediate assessment whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now. Place the person on their side if unresponsive.

redFlags.label: Possible stroke
redFlags.message: Sudden facial drooping, arm weakness or difficulty speaking is a stroke until proven otherwise. Treatment works only within a few hours.
redFlags.action: Call emergency services now and note the exact time symptoms began.

redFlags.label: Seizure
redFlags.message: A first seizure needs assessment to find the cause and to advise on driving and safety.
redFlags.action: Seek urgent assessment today. Call emergency services if the seizure lasted over five minutes or a second one followed.

redFlags.label: Significant gastrointestinal bleeding
redFlags.message: Vomiting blood, or passing black tarry stools, means bleeding inside the digestive tract.
redFlags.action: Go to an emergency department now.

redFlags.label: New jaundice
redFlags.message: Yellowing of the skin or eyes always needs blood tests to find out why.

redFlags.label: Sudden loss of vision
redFlags.message: Sight lost suddenly in one or both eyes needs assessment the same hour, whatever the cause.
redFlags.action: Go to an eye emergency department now.

redFlags.label: Thoughts of self-harm
redFlags.message: Thoughts of harming yourself or of being better off dead deserve help today. You do not have to be in crisis to reach out.
redFlags.action: Contact your doctor, a crisis line, or go to an emergency department now. If you are in immediate danger, call emergency services.

redFlags.label: New confusion coming on over hours or days
redFlags.message: Confusion that has come on over hours or days, or that comes and goes through the day, is delirium until proven otherwise. It is caused by something else -- an infection, a drug, pain, retention -- and that cause needs finding today.
redFlags.action: Seek same-day medical assessment. Take a list of all medications. Call emergency services if they are drowsy, feverish or cannot be roused properly.

disclaimer: This tool provides information about possible causes of symptoms. It is not a diagnosis and it cannot examine you. It does not replace assessment by a qualified clinician. If you feel very unwell, or your symptoms are getting rapidly worse, seek medical help immediately regardless of what this tool says.
